Class 5 · Module 2 — The Core Panels

Beyond Good and Bad Cholesterol: The Lipid Panel

Reading LDL, HDL, and triglycerides as a pattern — and knowing which ones actually move.

60 min read 8 cited sources

Two people walk out of the same lab with the same LDL cholesterol: 130 mg/dL. The first has an HDL of 65 and triglycerides of 70. The second has an HDL of 34 and triglycerides of 280. The report flags neither LDL value — both sit in the same "borderline" bucket — yet these two panels describe very different metabolic situations, and over a lifetime, very different cardiovascular trajectories. If you only read the LDL line, you would treat them the same. That is the central failure of the "good cholesterol / bad cholesterol" cartoon: it turns a rich, interacting pattern into a two-column scoreboard.

This chapter replaces the scoreboard with a working model. You will learn what LDL, HDL, and triglycerides actually represent, why non-HDL cholesterol and the ratios often tell a cleaner story than any single number, how the fasting question changes what you can conclude, and — the practical payoff — which lifestyle changes reliably shift which lipids, and by roughly how much.

First, the actionable version

Before the mechanisms, here is the decision-making frame this chapter builds toward. Keep it in view; everything that follows is justification and nuance.

  • Read the pattern, not the LDL line. The combination of LDL, HDL, and triglycerides carries more information than any one of them alone.
  • Compute non-HDL cholesterol in your head: total cholesterol minus HDL. It captures all the atherogenic particles, and it is valid whether or not you fasted.
  • Treat cardiovascular cut-points as risk thresholds, not percentiles. Unlike many markers we've discussed, the important lipid lines come from outcome research — they mark where risk rises, not where you fall relative to the population (recall Chapter 1).
  • Match the intervention to the marker. Triglycerides respond fast to carbohydrate and alcohol; HDL responds modestly to sustained aerobic training; LDL is comparatively stubborn to lifestyle alone.
  • Markedly abnormal values are a reason to see a clinician, not a puzzle to solve on a spreadsheet. This chapter helps you interpret — not diagnose or treat.
Think About It

Return to the two panels in the hook. Without reading further, which patient's picture worries you more, and which single number that the report didn't flag is doing most of the work in your judgment?

What the three headline numbers actually are

Cholesterol and triglycerides are fats; blood is water. To travel through plasma they ride inside lipoproteins — spherical particles with a water-friendly shell wrapped around a fatty core. The names on your lab report don't describe different kinds of cholesterol; they describe different vehicles carrying it. This is the single most clarifying idea in the whole panel.

LDL: the delivery fleet that gets stuck in the wall

Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles carry cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues. Your "LDL cholesterol" (LDL-C) is an estimate of how much cholesterol is riding in that fleet. It matters because LDL particles are small enough to slip into the artery wall, where — over years — they can be retained, oxidized, and drive the plaque-building process we call atherosclerosis.

This is not a soft association. The European Atherosclerosis Society's consensus panel assembled genetic (Mendelian randomization), epidemiologic, and randomized-trial evidence and concluded that LDL is not merely correlated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) but causally drives it, in proportion to how much LDL you're exposed to and for how long (Ference et al., 2017). The key word is cumulative: it's the area under the curve of LDL over a lifetime, not any single reading, that shapes risk. That reframes an "optimal" LDL as a long game, not a snapshot to fix once.

One honest caveat the same panel raises: LDL-C is a surrogate. The true driver is the number of atherogenic particles — measured more directly as apolipoprotein B (apoB), since each such particle carries one apoB molecule. When triglycerides are high or LDL is low, LDL-C and apoB can disagree. You don't need apoB to read a standard panel well, but it explains why non-HDL (below) is a smarter summary than LDL alone.

HDL: a marker of a process, not a magic scrubber

High-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles participate in returning cholesterol from tissues back toward the liver — "reverse cholesterol transport." Higher HDL-C tracks with lower cardiovascular risk in population studies, which is where "good cholesterol" comes from. But the story is subtler than the nickname. Trials and genetic studies that raise HDL pharmacologically have largely failed to reduce events, which tells us HDL-C is better understood as a marker of a favorable metabolic state than as something you benefit from by pushing higher for its own sake. Very high HDL is not automatically "better," and chasing an HDL number is not a therapeutic goal.

Practically: read HDL as context. A robust HDL alongside low triglycerides paints a reassuring metabolic picture. A low HDL alongside high triglycerides is one of the most common signatures of insulin resistance — and it's the triglyceride-HDL relationship, not HDL alone, that carries the signal.

Triglycerides: the fast-moving metabolic weather vane

Triglycerides (TG) are the body's main fat-storage and fat-transport molecule. In the fasting state they mostly ride in VLDL particles made by the liver; after a meal they surge inside dietary particles. Two things make TG uniquely useful. First, they are the most responsive lipid to short-term diet, alcohol, and body-fat changes — a weather vane rather than a climate record. Second, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and their leftover "remnant" particles are themselves atherogenic and independently predict cardiovascular risk (Nordestgaard & Varbo, 2014).

That review makes a point that echoes Chapter 1: the common triglyceride cut-points are risk thresholds derived from outcome data, not population percentiles. The line isn't "where most people sit"; it's "where risk starts climbing." Keep that distinction — it changes how you talk about a "high-normal" result.

Think About It

If someone tells you their HDL "improved" from 42 to 48 after a month, what would you want to know about their triglycerides and their recent training before you decide whether anything meaningful actually changed?

Non-HDL and the ratios: a cleaner story than any single number

Here's the move that upgrades you from scoreboard-reader to pattern-reader. Every atherogenic particle — LDL, VLDL, remnants, and the rest — carries cholesterol and one apoB. HDL is the only major fraction that isn't. So if you take total cholesterol and subtract HDL, what remains — non-HDL cholesterol — is the cholesterol carried by all the particles you'd rather have less of, in one number.

That single subtraction fixes two weaknesses of LDL-C at once. It captures the atherogenic contribution of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins that LDL-C ignores, and — because it's computed from total cholesterol and HDL, both stable after meals — it doesn't require fasting. The Multinational Cardiovascular Risk Consortium, pooling data from 19 countries, showed non-HDL-C is strongly and independently associated with long-term ASCVD across the entire concentration range, and built an individual risk tool around it (Brunner et al., 2019). Encouragingly for the behavioral theme of this course, they estimated that a 50% reduction in non-HDL-C was associated with meaningfully lower risk by age 75 — with more benefit the earlier it happens. Cumulative exposure, again.

The ratios

Ratios do something related: they let two numbers interrogate each other. The two most useful:

  • Total cholesterol ÷ HDL (TC/HDL). A compact summary of atherogenic-to-protective balance. Lower is more favorable; broadly, values under ~3.5 are reassuring and above ~5 warrant attention, but treat these as orientation, not verdicts.
  • Triglycerides ÷ HDL (TG/HDL). Not a formal decision limit, but a widely used flag for insulin resistance and small, dense LDL particles. A high ratio (driven by high TG and low HDL together) frequently accompanies the metabolic pattern that matters most.

The reason these matter is exactly the hook: they explain why the same LDL of 130 reads differently depending on its neighbors. LDL 130 with HDL 65 and TG 70 gives a non-HDL of 144 and a TC/HDL near 3.2 — a benign-looking pattern. LDL 130 with HDL 34 and TG 280 gives a non-HDL near 186 and a TC/HDL above 6 — a very different animal. Same flagged number; opposite stories.

Fasting or not? What it changes — and what it doesn't

For decades, lab slips said "fast 9–12 hours." The evidence no longer supports that as a routine requirement. A joint consensus of the European Atherosclerosis Society and the European Federation of Clinical Chemistry (Nordestgaard et al., 2016) evaluated fasting versus non-fasting profiles head-to-head and found the maximal average post-meal changes clinically trivial for most markers: total cholesterol drifts about −8 mg/dL, and triglycerides rise at most about +26 mg/dL. HDL and non-HDL barely move. Their recommendation: non-fasting is fine for routine lipid testing, with fasting reserved for specific situations — most notably when a non-fasting triglyceride comes back very high (they suggest re-checking fasting above ~440 mg/dL).

Two practical consequences. First, the marker least disturbed by meals — non-HDL — is also the one carrying the cleanest risk signal, which is a happy alignment. Second, the marker most disturbed by meals is triglycerides, so triglycerides are where the fasting question actually bites.

The nuance: non-fasting TG may be a feature, not a bug

Because we spend most of our waking hours in a fed or partly fed state, some researchers argue that a non-fasting triglyceride — drawn within a few hours of eating — reflects your typical metabolic reality better than an artificially fasted one, and may predict cardiovascular risk at least as well (Farrell et al., 2021). The catch is standardization: "non-fasting" spans everything from a black coffee to a large pizza, so an unstructured non-fasting TG can misclassify if you don't know what preceded it. The workable rule: for trend-tracking, be consistent — compare fasting to fasting, or same-conditions to same-conditions — and treat a single high non-fasting TG as a prompt to recheck under known conditions, not a conclusion.

Think About It

A client's triglycerides jump from 110 to 180 between two draws. Before concluding anything shifted metabolically, what one question about the second morning would you ask first?

What actually shifts — matching interventions to markers

This is where lipids earn their place as the course's flagship "what actually moves" panel. Unlike some markers that barely budge with lifestyle, lipids — especially triglycerides — are genuinely responsive. But the responsiveness is uneven: each intervention hits some fractions hard and others barely at all. Reading the evidence honestly means naming both the effect and its size, and separating well-supported effects from popular overreach.

Triglycerides: the responsive one (carbohydrate and alcohol)

If you want a lipid to move quickly, target triglycerides. The mechanism is direct: excess dietary carbohydrate — particularly refined, rapidly absorbed carbohydrate — and alcohol both push the liver to make more VLDL. Parks (2001) documented carbohydrate-induced hypertriglyceridemia: when carbohydrate climbs past roughly 55% of energy, fasting triglycerides rise even as dietary fat falls, and the effect can emerge within about five days. Reverse the input and triglycerides typically fall just as briskly. Alcohol works through a related hepatic pathway; cutting a heavy or even moderate habit often drops triglycerides substantially. These are among the best-supported, fastest lipid responses you will see.

HDL: modest, and mostly aerobic

HDL responds to sustained aerobic training — but keep expectations calibrated. Kodama et al.'s (2007) meta-analysis of 35 randomized trials (n = 1,404) found a mean net HDL increase of just 2.53 mg/dL. The moderators are instructive: every extra 10 minutes of exercise per session added roughly 1.4 mg/dL, with a threshold around 120 minutes (or ~900 kcal) of aerobic work per week before much happened — and session duration mattered more than intensity or frequency. A more recent meta-analysis in people with overweight or obesity (Cao et al., 2025) reinforced the nuance: both moderate and vigorous aerobic exercise lowered TG, TC, and LDL, but only moderate-intensity exercise reliably raised HDL. So the honest coaching message is: aerobic training nudges HDL up a little and improves the whole panel modestly — real, worthwhile, but measured in single digits, not transformation.

LDL: the stubborn one

LDL-C is the least responsive of the three to lifestyle alone. Aerobic training produces a meaningful-but-limited reduction (Cao et al., 2025 reported a standardized mean difference of about −0.42 in overweight/obese participants), and dietary patterns that cut saturated fat and add viscous fiber and plant sterols can lower it further. But relative to what pharmacotherapy achieves, and relative to how much triglycerides can swing, LDL is comparatively fixed by genetics and hepatic biology. This is exactly where popular overreach lives — claims that a particular diet "reversed" a high LDL should be read skeptically. The realistic frame: lifestyle can move LDL somewhat, and every bit matters over a lifetime of cumulative exposure (Ference et al., 2017), but a markedly elevated LDL that won't budge is a reason for medical evaluation, not a lifestyle failure.

Weight change: the multiplier

Loss of excess body fat improves the whole pattern, with the largest proportional effect on triglycerides and a helpful lift to HDL and reduction in LDL. Cao et al. (2025) found broad improvement across all four fractions with aerobic exercise in overweight and obese participants. Weight loss tends to amplify the other levers rather than act alone.

The evidence indicates that LDL causes atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and that the benefit of lowering LDL is determined by both the magnitude and the duration of the reduction.

The age-and-life-stage lens: what "optimal" means when

Chapter 2 warned against a single "optimal" for every age. Lipids make the point vividly. Because risk from LDL and non-HDL is cumulative, a given number carries different weight at 30 than at 65. A modestly elevated non-HDL at 30 represents decades of future exposure — arguably more reason to act early, since Brunner et al. (2019) found the benefit of reduction is greatest when it starts young. The same number first appearing at 70, in someone with a long healthy history, is read in a different context.

Physiology shifts too. Triglycerides and total cholesterol tend to drift up through midlife; HDL patterns differ by sex and change around menopause. None of this means you lower the bar with age — the risk thresholds don't relax — but it does mean interpretation is contextual. "In range for your age group" is a statement about the population you resemble; "optimal for your trajectory" is a statement about lifetime exposure. They are not the same, and where exactly "optimal" sits — how low is low enough, for whom — remains genuinely debated at the edges.

Think About It

Two people share a non-HDL of 160: one is 28, the other 68. Why might the younger person have more to gain from acting on it, even though the older person is at higher near-term risk?

When the panel says "see someone"

This chapter teaches interpretation, not diagnosis. Certain findings are signposts to professional evaluation rather than self-management: a very high LDL that suggests possible familial hypercholesterolemia (often flagged when LDL persistently sits well above ~190 mg/dL, especially with a family history of early heart disease); triglycerides high enough to threaten the pancreas (well into the hundreds and beyond); or a pattern that doesn't respond to sincere, sustained lifestyle change. The right move in each case is a clinician who can weigh the full picture — including markers beyond this panel, family history, and overall risk — and decide whether treatment is warranted. Reading your bloodwork well includes knowing when reading isn't enough.

Key Takeaways

  • LDL, HDL, and triglycerides name lipoprotein vehicles, not different cholesterols; read them as an interacting pattern, not a two-column scoreboard.
  • Non-HDL cholesterol (total minus HDL) captures every atherogenic particle in one number, needs no fasting, and often tells a cleaner story than LDL alone (Brunner et al., 2019).
  • LDL causes ASCVD in proportion to cumulative lifetime exposure — making early, sustained action more valuable than any single reading (Ference et al., 2017).
  • Non-fasting testing is fine for routine panels; fasting mainly matters for triglycerides, and even then chiefly to confirm a very high non-fasting result (Nordestgaard et al., 2016; Farrell et al., 2021).
  • Match the lever to the marker: triglycerides move fast with carbohydrate and alcohol (Parks, 2001; Nordestgaard & Varbo, 2014); HDL rises modestly with aerobic training (Kodama et al., 2007; Cao et al., 2025); LDL is comparatively stubborn to lifestyle alone.
  • Cardiovascular cut-points are risk thresholds from outcome data, not population percentiles — and "optimal" is read through the lens of age and lifetime trajectory.
  • Markedly abnormal values are a reason for medical evaluation, not a diagnosis exercise.
Looking Ahead

Lipids told us about cardiovascular risk over decades; next we turn to a panel that reports on the here-and-now of fuel handling. Chapter 6 tackles glucose and insulin — fasting glucose, HbA1c, and the early-warning markers of insulin resistance — where, once again, "in range" and "optimal" part ways, and where the triglyceride-HDL pattern you just learned will reappear as an unexpected clue.
